Ménière
Disease
NRBS 4210: Professional Nursing 
Practice with Adult Clients III
College of Nursing, Downstate Health 
Sciences University
David Addesso, Marzan Amir, Edwin 
Gutierrez, Kohei Tetsuka, and Shella Yazdi

WHAT IS MÉNIÈRE DISEASE?
● It is a rare inner ear problem that causes 
dizziness, hearing loss, tinnitus, and a feeling 
of pressure. This is typically in one ear 
(Cleveland Clinic, 2025).
● In the inner ear, endolymphatic hydrops 
(abnormal fluid build up) causes increased 
pressure or rupture of the inner ear 
membrane, leading to the symptoms of 
Ménière’s disease.
● This disease affects approximately 12 out of 
every 1,000 people in the United States. 
Approximately 45,000 new cases are 
diagnosed each year  (NIDCD, 2017a).

RISK FACTORS & PREVENTION
RISK FACTORS: 
● Age: it often affects people from the range of 40 to 6o years old.
● Genes: About 7% to 10% of people with Ménière’s disease have a family 
history of the disorder. The condition can be inherited.
● Autoimmune diseases: Autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis 
(RA), lupus and ankylosing spondylitis are a likelihood indicator of this 
disease. 
● Conditions that may cause too much endolymph to build such as allergies, 
inner ear blockages, head injuries, infections, and migraine headaches.
PREVENTION: 
● The cause of this disease is unknown. Although researchers can conclude 
that it corresponds with fluid buildup in the inner ear, the reason as to why 
is still not known. “It's considered to be a lifelong condition” (Mayo Clinic 
Staff, 2026).

HEALTH PROMOTION & EARLY DETECTION
IMPORTANCE OF EARLY DETECTION
● In recognizing cues/symptoms of Ménière Disease, patients are responsible for being apart of their 
role in managing symptoms, improve/maintain hearing quality, and improving their quality of life. 
CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
● Vertigo: These are known as dizzy spills. Some clients may have “drop attacks”. This occurs when the 
vertigo is intense causing imbalance to the client to which they could fall.
● Hearing trouble/loss: This disease typically affects in one ear. It steadily starts as difficulty in hearing 
low noises. Without any treatment or management, hearing loss can be further worsened. 
● Tinnitus: This is often ringing in the ear. It can cause discomfort to clients.
● Feeling of pressure : Clients often describe their ear feeling full or heavy due to a feeling of weighted 
pressure causing discomfort. You may feel pressure or fullness in the affected ear.
● Nausea and vomiting (Cleveland Clinic, 2025).
IMPORTANCE OF EARLY DETECTION
● As soon as these symptoms occur, it is imperative that the client notifies their provider and begins 
diagnostic testing. 
● After testing, proper treatment can be arranged as hearing loss worsening can be an effect on little to 
no management. 
● Although this diseases is idiopathic, treatments can help manage symptoms and lessen the effects 
Meniere's disease on the client’s daily life. (Mayo Clinic Staff, 2026).

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
Diagnostic criteria: at least two spontaneous vertigo attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, 
hearing loss confirmed by a hearing test, and hearing changes, ringing, or fullness that 
fluctuate in the affected ear. Other conditions that could explain these symptoms must be 
excluded (NIDCD, 2024).
History and physical exam:any vertigo episodes? Hearing changes? tinnitus or ear fullness? 
These findings help identify characteristic patterns because there is no single test that 
confirms Ménière’s disease (NIDCD, 2024).
Audiometry (hearing test): tests how well patient hears sounds at different frequencies. 
People with Ménière’s disease will commonly have difficulty hearing low and medium pitched 
sounds (Basura et al., 2020).
Weber test: Determines sensorineural hearing loss (affecting inner ear). A tuning fork placed 
at the center of the head may sound louder in the unaffected ear (Hinkle et al., 2025).
MRI: to exclude other possible causes of hearing loss and dizziness such as a tumor  (NIDCD, 
2024).
Additional testing:Electronystagmography (ENG) records eye movements to assess inner ear 
balance function. Electrocochleography measures electrical responses to sound from the 
inner ear and hearing nerve.(CN VIII)

ASSESSMENT - WARNING SIGNS
● Attack history: onset, frequency, duration, severity. Most patients feel fine between 
attacks but some notice lingering feeling of unsteadiness, changes in hearing, ringing in 
the ears, or a feeling of fullness in the ear (Hinkle et al., 2025).
● Past medications and treatments: have they previously tried anything for vertigo and 
did anything help? (Hinkle et al., 2025)
● Fall risk: observe balance and walking. Perform Romberg testby having pt stand with 
feet together first with eyes open, then closed. Pts with impaired balance may sway 
more with eyes close. Take caution and stay close to prevent falls. (Hinkle et al., 2025)
● Eye movements: observe for nystagmus (jerky eye movements), which may accompany 
inner-ear balance disturbances (Hinkle et al., 2025) 
● ADLs: Assess if the pt can bathe, dress, and eat safely and independently 
● Concerning findings: watch out for dehydration findings including dry mouth, 
orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia. Especially concerning during active attack and the 
patient is vomiting and not drinking enough (Hinkle et al., 2025)

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
Many patients with Ménière disease can be successfully treated with diet and medication. 
○ Symptoms can be controlled by adhering to a low-sodium (less than 2,000 mg/d)
■ Limit foods high in salt or sugar
■ Eat meals and snacks at regular intervals 
■ Drink plenty of water daily
■ Limit alcohol intake 
○ The amount of sodium in the body is one of the main factors regulating the balance of fluid in 
the body 
○ Sodium and fluid retention disrupts the balance between the endolymph and perilymph in 
the inner ear 
● Patients with Ménière disease often report impaired quality of life 
○ Monitor for anxiety and depression 
○ Psychological evaluation and cognitive therapy may be indicated 
● Patients with persistent vertigo spells can use a Meniett device 
○ A doctor must insert a tympanostomy tube (small ventilation stub) which connects to a
specialized ear-cuff 
○ Portable generator sends gentle intermittent air-pressure pulses to help displace excess 
inner ear fluid and normalize pressure balance

MEDICATION MANAGEMENT
Pharmacologic therapy for Ménière disease:
● Antihistamines and antiemetic 
○ Meclizine & Promethazine to relieve nausea and vomiting 
● Tranquilizers 
○ Diazepam can be used in acute circumstances to help 
control anxiety
● Diuretic therapy 
○ (e.g. Hydrochlorothiazide, Triamterene, and 
Spironolactone)
○ May relieve symptoms by lowering pressure in the 
endolymphatic system
● Intratympanic Injection 
○ Gentamicin is used to cause ablation of the vestibular hair 
cells
■ Risk of hearing loss is high, while evidence of efficacy 
is uncertain

Surgical Management
Although many patients respond very well to a more conservative approach to 
therapy, some still attacks of vertigo that could be disabling. 
● If the attacks reduce their quality of life, patients may elect to undergo surgery.
Endolymphatic Sac 
Decompression
● Also known as shunting 
● A drain is inserted in 
the endolymphatic sac 
through a postauricular 
incision
● First line (simple done 
in outpatient)
Labyrinthectomy
● Performed by opening the 
inner ear and destroying the 
soft tissue or drilling out the 
bone and removing the 
entire labyrinth
● Destroys the hearing of the 
inner ear 
○ Not an option if the 
affected  ear has 
adequate hearing 
Vestibular Nerve Sectioning
● Provides greatest success 
rate (98%)
● Severs the balance nerve 
to the brain 
● Can eliminate vertigo 
while potentially 
preserving hearing 
○ Depending on the 
surgical approach 
and pt’s existing 
hearing status

NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES
Pharmacologic Therapy
● Meclizine/promethazine
○ Monitor for drowsiness and fatigue
○ Implement fall precautions
○ Regularly assess respiratory status
○ Monitor for EPS for promethazine
○ Assess for anticholinergic effects
● Diazepam
○ Check vitals before and after administration
○ Assess level of anxiety of the patient during an 
attack
○ Implement fall precautions
○ Assess for respiratory depression
○ Have flumazenil ready (reversal agent)
● Diuretics
○ Check vitals before and after administration
○ Monitor electrolyte levels
○ Administer in the morning
○ Track I&O and daily weight
Perioperative care
● Preoperative
○ Obtain baseline hearing, balance, cranial 
nerve function and vital signs
○ Provide nursing care during acute 
attacks
○ Reassure and provide emotional support 
for the patient
● Postoperative care
○ Safety/fall precautions
○ Monitor for hearing acuity
○ Cranial nerve monitoring
○ Manage symptoms
○ Wound site care

PATIENT & FAMILY EDUCATION
● Diet and Lifestyle changes
○ Limit salt intake to 1,500 to 2,000 mg may reduce symptoms 
○ Limit smoking and caffeine 
○ Stay hydrated
● Psychological changes
○ Many who have this disease often report increased anxiety and 
depression 
● Pharmacological 
○ Aspirin or aspirin-containing medications may increase tinnitus and 
dizziness 
● Vertigo
○ Restrict activity during spells of vertigo
○ Identify possible hazards in the home environment
○ Positional changes may aid in preventing injury

DISCHARGE PLANNING & HOMECARE
Discharge Planning
● Pt education on the chronic nature and clinical manifestations of Meniere’s
● Dietary Modification: Encourage a low sodium diet (1,500-2,000 mg/day) and 
avoiding foods with MSG (monosodium glutamate)
● Lifestyle Modifications: Limit caffeine, alcohol, smoking and manage stress
● Medication adherence and follow up care
● Monitoring: Diary documenting frequency, duration, severity and triggers of 
vertigo episodes.
Home Care
● Fall prevention: remove clutter, loose rugs, improved lighting, handrails
● Slow position changes
● Avoid intensive or high risk activity during episodes
● During episode sit or lie down immediately and rest in a quiet/dark room
● Assistive devices as needed
● Family education on how to assist during episodes

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION #1
A nurse is caring for a 58 year old client diagnosed with Meniere’s disease who is experiencing 
an acute episode of vertigo. The client reports nausea and tinnitus and has vomited several 
times. Assessment findings include a blood pressure of 94/58 mmHg, heart rate of 112 
beats/min and dry mucous membrane.
Which nursing intervention should the nurse prioritize?
a) Administer prescribed meclizine to reduce vertigo and nausea.
b) Assist the client into a safe resting position, implement fall precautions, and assess 
hydration status.
c) Educate the client about maintaining a sodium intake below 2,000 mg/day
d) Perform a Romberg test to evaluate the severity of the clients balance impairment.

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION #1 ANSWER
B. Assist the client into a safe resting position, implement 
fall precautions and assess hydration status.
Rationale: Immediate priorities are preventing injury and 
recognizing possible dehydration from repeated vomiting. 
Hypotension, tachycardia and dry mucous membranes 
suggest volume depletion.

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION #2
The nurse is educating a client with Meniere’s disease who is recommended 
to follow the Hydrops diet. Which of the following guidelines included are 
included in this diet? Select all that apply.
A. Even food intake throughout the day 
B. Avoid high salt content
C. Limit alcohol
D. Double fiber intake
E. Avoiding foods with MSG

NCLEX-STYLE QUESTION #2 ANSWER
Answer: A, B, C, E
Rationale: 
A: Consistent meal timing is recommended in maintaining consistent blood glucose and fluid 
balance reducing fluctuations in ear fluid pressure.
B: Restricting sodium helps reduce fluid retention which can worsen endolymphatic hydrops
C: Limiting alcohol is recommended for symptoms management because it can affect ear fluid 
regulation
D: Although fiber intake promotes GI health it does not specifically address endolymphatic 
hydrops or inner ear fluid regulation. 
E:  MSG is a sodium containing flavor enhancer commonly found in processed foods.
